task1-chart.title: Task 1: Bar chart and line graph reports
task1-chart.summary: The examiner is testing whether you can select and report the key features, not copy the data. A clear overview, accurate figures and sensible comparisons are what move you from Band 6 to 7 and beyond.
steps: Read the title, axes, units and time frame first. Write down what is measured (for example percentage of commuters, thousand visitors) and the dates, because these decide your tense and your paraphrase.
Scan for the single biggest movement or difference: the highest and lowest items, the steepest rise or fall, any crossing point. Mark two or three of these only; everything else is secondary.

Decide your grouping before writing: by trend (those that rose versus those that fell), by rank (leaders versus the rest) or by time (before and after a turning point). Each body paragraph needs one logical group.

Draft the overview in your head as two sentences with no numbers: the main trend or difference, then a contrast or stand-out item. If you cannot say it without figures, you have not yet selected the key features.
Pick the figures that prove your overview (start, end, peak, trough, biggest gap) and ignore the rest. Check units and the direction of each change before you write a single number.

structure.purpose: Show what the visual contains in your own words, in one sentence, with no opinion or data.
sentences: Paraphrase: change the verb (shows to compares or illustrates), the measure (number to figure or proportion) and the time phrase, but keep the facts identical.

structure.purpose: Give the reader the main story so the detail that follows has a frame. This is the paragraph examiners look for first.
sentences: Overview: main feature: the largest trend or difference, with no numbers.
Overview: second feature: a contrast, a second trend or a stand-out item, still without detailed figures.

structure.purpose: Report the first logical group of data with selected, accurate figures and at least one comparison.
sentences: Topic sentence: name the group and its main direction.
Key figures: exact start and end values with units for the main item.
Comparison: set it against another item with whereas, while or a comparative form.
Trend detail: add the shape of the change, such as a peak, steady rise or sharp fall.

structure.purpose: Report the remaining group, linking back to Body 1 so the report reads as one piece, not two lists.
sentences: Topic sentence: introduce the second group and how it differs from the first.
Key figures: exact values with units for its main item.
Comparison: contrast with the first group or another item in this one.
Closing detail: one further notable point, for instance a rank change; no conclusion is needed.

timing.what: Analyse the visual, choose the overview features and decide the grouping
Write: introduction and overview first (4 minutes), then two body paragraphs
Check units, figures, tenses, and that the overview contains no numbers

pitfalls: Writing no overview, or burying it in the last paragraph. Task Achievement is capped at around Band 5 without a clear overview, because you have not shown you can see the whole picture.
Listing every figure item by item. This reads as copying the chart, produces a flat list and fails the instruction to select main features, which limits both Task Achievement and Coherence.
Giving reasons or opinions (the council must have invested in cycling). The task is to report, and invented causes are unsupported information that examiners penalise.
Misreading units or mixing up values, such as writing 6 per cent as 6 thousand. Inaccurate data is a Task Achievement error, however good the language is.
Using one tense or one trend verb throughout (rose, rose, rose). A narrow range of vocabulary and structures caps Lexical Resource and Grammatical Range at Band 6.
Copying the question wording in the introduction. Copied words are not counted towards your assessment, and they signal limited paraphrasing ability.

phrases: the gap between X and Y narrowed
The most striking feature is that
X remained the most popular throughout
In contrast to the general trend,

band8: Task Achievement: the overview is a genuine synthesis (main trend plus a significant contrast), and every figure in the body supports it. At Band 7 the overview is present but the body lists data without ranking importance.

Task Achievement: data are grouped by meaning (for example those that rose against those that fell) rather than in the order of the legend. Band 8 shows selection; Band 7 often reports everything once.
Coherence and Cohesion: each body paragraph has a topic sentence, and the second links back to the first with a contrast or reference so the report reads as one argument, not a series of facts.
Lexical Resource: varied, precise trend vocabulary and approximation (a marginal rise, just under a fifth), with no repeated verbs and no loose words such as 'big' or 'a lot'.
Grammatical Range and Accuracy: a mix of comparative structures, participle clauses (Having peaked at 95, attendance fell...) and relative clauses, with figures, units and prepositions all accurate.

task1-process.title: Task 1: Process diagrams
task1-process.summary: The examiner is testing whether you can describe a sequence accurately and completely, using sequencing language and the passive voice, while still giving an overview of the whole process.
steps: Identify whether the diagram is a natural cycle or a manufacturing process, whether it is linear or cyclical, and where it starts and ends. The overview depends on this.
Number every stage and note the inputs, the action and the output at each one. Missing a stage is a Task Achievement error, so count carefully.
Decide how to group the stages into two or three phases (preparation, transformation, finishing). Each body paragraph should cover one phase, not a random half of the numbers.
Note which stages need the passive (most do, because the agent is a machine) and which tools, materials or equipment are named, so you reuse the exact labels accurately.
Plan the overview: the total number of stages, the start and end points, and one feature such as 'linear', 'cyclical' or 'dominated by mechanical treatment'.

structure.purpose: Say what the diagram shows and the process it describes, in your own words.
sentences: Paraphrase: use 'illustrates' or 'outlines', the number of stages, and the start and end points; replace stages and produce with synonyms.

structure.purpose: Summarise the process as a whole without describing any single step.
sentences: Overview: main feature: the process is linear or cyclical, with a clear start and end.
Overview: second feature: how the stages divide into phases, for example preparation then formation.

structure.purpose: Describe the first phase in order, with the passive and a different sequencing word at each step.
sentences: Topic sentence: name the phase and its purpose.
Key figures: the first one or two stages in order, with inputs and actions.
Comparison: distinguish between stages, using whereas or while, or show how one step prepares the next.
Trend detail: the method or equipment used and why, if the diagram shows it.

structure.purpose: Describe the remaining stages to the final product, ending clearly.
sentences: Topic sentence: name the second phase.
Key figures: the next stages in order with materials and results.
Comparison: contrast the roles of two stages in this phase.
Closing detail: the final stage and the end product.

timing.what: Number the stages, find start and end, decide the two phases
Write: introduction and overview (4 minutes), then two body paragraphs following the order exactly
Check no stage is missing, passive forms, and sequencing words are varied

pitfalls: Leaving out a stage or reordering stages. Process accuracy is the core of Task Achievement, and the examiner will check the sequence against the diagram.
Using only 'then' as a linker. Repetitive sequencing words keep Coherence and Cohesion at Band 6, and mechanical 'first, second, third' lists look rehearsed.
Writing in the active voice with 'they' or 'people' when the diagram shows machines or natural processes. This changes the meaning and weakens Grammatical Range.
Giving no overview, or writing an overview that simply repeats the first stage. Examiners need to see that you understand the process as a whole.
Adding information not on the diagram, such as why the recycling matters. It is irrelevant, and unsupported content costs Task Achievement.
Describing every minor detail, such as every label on a machine. Group related steps and focus on what changes the material.

phrases: The process can be divided into two phases
from raw materials to the finished product

band8: Task Achievement: all stages are present in the correct order, grouped into phases, and the overview names the shape of the process. Band 7 often covers every stage but without a phase structure.
Coherence and Cohesion: sequencing language is varied and precise (once, following this, at this point) and reference words connect stages, instead of a repeated 'then'.
Lexical Resource: technical vocabulary from the diagram is paraphrased accurately (screened, filtered out; heated rollers, heated cylinders) and collocations are natural.

Grammatical Range and Accuracy: accurate passives in several tenses and forms, with participle clauses and relative clauses (which is then dried) joining stages smoothly, with no error in verb agreement.

opinion.title: Task 2: Opinion (to what extent do you agree or disagree?)
opinion.summary: The examiner is testing whether you take and sustain a clear position on the exact statement given, support it with developed reasons, and show control of argument and language. A consistent, nuanced position is the biggest lever at Band 7 and above.
steps: Underline the command phrase ('To what extent do you agree or disagree?') and the key claim. This question wants a position on this statement, not a general essay on the topic.
Break the statement into its parts: the group, the action and any limiting words (such as 'even those unrelated'). Each limiting word is something you must address, not ignore.
Decide your position in 60 seconds: fully agree, fully disagree or partly agree. If partly, state exactly which part you accept and which you reject, so the position stays clear.

Choose two reasons that directly prove your position. For each, find a specific example (a field, a country, a type of person) and a result. Ideas you cannot develop in four sentences should be dropped.
Decide the role of Body 2: a second reason, or a counter-argument that you concede and then limit. Check that your thesis and your plan do not contradict each other.

structure.purpose: Frame the debate and commit to one clear position that answers the question as asked.
sentences: Background: paraphrase the topic neutrally, without copying the question.
Thesis: state your position with the question's key terms and your main reasons.
Outline: signal what each body paragraph will cover (optional).

structure.purpose: Present your strongest reason fully, so it reads as proven and not just asserted.
sentences: Topic sentence: one main idea that supports your position.
Explanation: explain why or how the idea holds.
Example: a specific, believable case.
Result or effect: what the example proves for the question.

structure.purpose: Add a second reason or deal with the strongest opposing point, and show it does not undermine your position.
sentences: Topic sentence: second reason or concession.
Explanation: develop the logic.
Example: a precise illustration.
Link: tie back to the question or limit the counter-argument.

structure.purpose: Confirm that your answer is consistent from start to finish, without new ideas.
sentences: Summary: restate position and two reasons in new words.
Final judgement: a short statement of the overall implication.

timing.what: Plan: underline command words, choose position, two reasons with examples
Write: introduction (4), body 1 (9), body 2 (9), conclusion (3), buffer (5)
Check: position consistent in thesis and conclusion, word count over 250, articles, agreement, spelling

pitfalls: Memorised or copied introductions. Examiners recognise templates, and copied words are discounted. It also tends to produce a generic thesis that does not answer the actual statement, reducing Task Response.
An unclear or shifting position, such as agreeing in the introduction and arguing the other side in the conclusion. Task Response needs a position that is clear throughout.

Answering only part of the statement. If it says 'even unrelated subjects', you must deal with that limit; ignoring it is a partial answer and limits Task Response to Band 5, where the task is only partially addressed.
Undeveloped ideas: a topic sentence and one generic example. Band 7 needs a reason that is extended and supported; a list of reasons with no development stays at Band 5 or 6.
Vague, unlikely examples ('some people say', 'in a country') that prove nothing. Specific, plausible cases are what make an argument credible.
Informal or over-emphatic language (a lot of, very very important, definitely 100 per cent). It reduces precision in Lexical Resource and sounds subjective in an academic essay.
Mechanical linking ('Firstly, Secondly, In addition, Moreover'). Overused connectors break Coherence and Cohesion, because ideas should be linked by logic and reference, not signposts.

phrases: I am largely in agreement with
I agree only to a limited extent that
This is not to say that

band8: Task Response: the position is nuanced and stated precisely (for example 'largely agree, with one qualification') and every paragraph, including the conclusion, serves it. At Band 7 the position is clear but ideas can drift.
Task Response: ideas are developed to a result or implication, so each example is explained as evidence, rather than only mentioned. Band 7 gives good ideas that stop after the example.
Coherence and Cohesion: progression is logical and cohesion is invisible: pronouns, substitution and topic-sentence links carry the argument, with few mechanical connectors.
Lexical Resource: precise, natural collocations (transferable skills, narrow specialisation) with little repetition of the question's words and rare, correct less common vocabulary.
Grammatical Range and Accuracy: most sentences are error-free, with a deliberate mix of conditionals, concessions, relative clauses and passives, and hedged claims.
Argument quality: a counter-argument is acknowledged and answered inside the essay, which shows evaluation rather than a one-sided list.

discussion.title: Task 2: Discussion (discuss both views and give your opinion)
discussion.summary: The examiner is testing three things at once: do you present both views fairly, do you give your own opinion, and is that opinion clear and consistent? Missing either view or the opinion is a partial answer.
steps: Underline 'Discuss both views' and 'give your own opinion'. These are two separate tasks, and you will be marked on both.
Write View A and View B in a few words each, so you know exactly what each side claims (for example, roads versus public transport).
Decide your own opinion before writing: which view you support, or whether you hold a balanced position. State it in the introduction and confirm it in the conclusion.
For each view, choose the strongest argument and a specific example. Give the view you reject a fair and credible case; a caricature is a weak argument and loses marks.
Decide where the opinion lives: usually in the thesis and conclusion, and woven into the body of the view you support. Check that it never contradicts either.

structure.purpose: Show you understand the debate, and declare your opinion so the reader reads the rest in context.
sentences: Background: paraphrase the debate neutrally.
Thesis: signal both views and state your own opinion.
Outline: what each paragraph will do (optional).

structure.purpose: Present View A fairly and fully, as its supporters would argue it.
sentences: Topic sentence: the view and its main claim.
Explanation: why its supporters believe it.
Example: a specific case where it works.
Result or effect: what that shows, including its limit if relevant.

structure.purpose: Present View B and show why you find it stronger (or why you hold a balanced view).
sentences: Topic sentence: the contrast with View A, using a concession marker.
Explanation: why this view holds.
Example: a specific case.
Result or effect: what follows, which supports your opinion.

structure.purpose: Weigh the two views and restate your opinion without adding new arguments.
sentences: Summary: acknowledge both views and the key difference between them.
Final judgement: your opinion, in new words.

timing.what: Plan: sum up both views, decide opinion, one reason and example for each view
Write: introduction (4), body 1 (9), body 2 (9), conclusion (3), buffer (5)
Check: both views covered, opinion visible in introduction and conclusion, no new ideas in conclusion

pitfalls: Describing only one view in depth, or giving one view a single sentence. Task Response needs both views to be discussed fully and fairly.
Forgetting to give an opinion, or hiding it in the final line only. The question asks for it directly, so omission is a partial answer capped at Band 5 to 6.
An opinion that contradicts the body (arguing strongly for roads and then concluding for public transport). A position that is not consistent damages Task Response and Coherence.
A weak, strawman case for the view you reject. Examiners reward a balanced discussion; an unfair one reads as one-sided.
Treating the question as 'which is better' with no nuance. At higher bands, you can qualify the opinion (public transport first, roads where no alternative exists).
Vague examples ('in some countries'). Specific, plausible cases give credibility and are a mark of a Band 7 or 8 answer.
Repeating the same linking word to open both bodies. Use contrast markers with a purpose and vary how the paragraphs begin.

phrases: Those in favour of ... point out that
I find the second view more persuasive because

band8: Task Response: both views are given equal intellectual weight with their own best argument, and the opinion emerges from the weighing, not just announced. At Band 7 the second view is often thinner.
Task Response: the opinion is nuanced and conditional (invest in transit, use roads selectively), which shows judgement rather than a binary choice.
Coherence and Cohesion: the two bodies mirror each other in structure, and contrast markers and reference words make the comparison clear without mechanical signposts.
Lexical Resource: neutral reporting verbs (contend, maintain, point out) and precise topic vocabulary (congestion, modal shift, commuters) replace repeated 'think' and 'good'.
Grammatical Range and Accuracy: concession structures (While some argue ..., I believe ...), participles and relative clauses are accurate and varied, with few errors.

problem-solution.title: Task 2: Problem and solution (causes and solutions)
problem-solution.summary: The examiner is testing whether you answer every part (causes or problems, and solutions) with ideas that match each other. Solutions must be realistic, specific and linked to the causes you identified.
steps: Underline each question word: 'what are the main causes' and 'what solutions could be introduced'. This is two tasks, and both need roughly equal development.
Identify the exact problem in the prompt (less physical activity) and its direction, so your causes explain that trend and not a different one.
List three or four causes quickly, then choose the one or two that are most significant and that you can link directly to a solution. Quality of development beats quantity.
For each solution, name who acts (government, employers, schools) and how it works. A solution without an agent or mechanism is only a wish.
Check the match: each solution should clearly respond to a cause you wrote about. Mark the connections in your plan before you start writing.

structure.purpose: Set up the problem and promise a structured answer to both parts.
sentences: Background: paraphrase the trend in neutral terms.
Thesis: signal the causes and your main solutions.
Outline: say how the essay is organised (optional).

structure.purpose: Explain the most significant cause or causes in depth, with evidence and consequences.
sentences: Topic sentence: the main cause.
Explanation: how it produces the problem.
Example: a specific, plausible situation.
Result or effect: the consequence for people or society.

structure.purpose: Offer practical solutions that respond directly to the causes, showing who acts and how.
sentences: Topic sentence: the main solution, with its link to the cause.
Explanation: how it works.
Example: where it has worked or could work.
Result or effect: a complementary measure or its outcome.

structure.purpose: Pull causes and solutions together and show why action matters.
sentences: Summary: restate the cause and the solution in new words.
Final judgement: the implication or priority.

timing.what: Plan: identify the parts, select main causes, match each with a solution, add examples
Write: introduction (4), causes (9), solutions (9), conclusion (3), buffer (5)
Check: both parts answered, solutions match causes, word count, grammar

pitfalls: Answering only causes, or only solutions, or giving a one-sentence solution. Both parts of the question must be developed, or Task Response is limited to Band 5.
Solutions that do not match the causes you identified. Examiners read this as weak logic, damaging Task Response and Coherence.
Unrealistic or vague solutions ('the government should do something', 'everyone should exercise more'). Specific, workable measures with an agent are expected.
Listing four or five causes in one sentence each. That is undeveloped; two well-explained causes score higher than five named ones.
Blaming people with moral language (lazy, selfish). It is subjective and informal, and it reduces the academic tone required.
Confusing cause and effect (listing obesity as a cause of inactivity), which signals poor control of ideas.
A conclusion that adds new solutions. The conclusion should only summarise.

phrases: A more effective approach would be to
could go a long way towards
In many suburban areas, for instance,

band8: Task Response: solutions are explicitly linked to causes with a clear mechanism (redesign towns, so walking becomes realistic), and feasibility is acknowledged. Band 7 offers sound but generic solutions.
Task Response: ideas are developed through to consequences, and at least one claim is hedged or qualified to show judgement.
Coherence and Cohesion: the essay is organised problem to solution with clear signalling, and each paragraph ends with a result that leads into the next.
Lexical Resource: topic-specific, precise vocabulary (sedentary occupations, active travel, segregated cycle lanes) rather than common words (not moving, bike roads).
Grammatical Range and Accuracy: complex sentences including conditionals, passives and noun phrases are used accurately for cause and effect, with few slips.

two-part.title: Task 2: Two-part question
two-part.summary: The examiner is testing whether you answer two different questions separately and fully. The challenge is balance: each question needs its own developed paragraph, and the thesis must answer both.
steps: Underline both questions and identify their types: one may ask for reasons ('Why...?') and the other for a judgement ('Should...?'). Each demands a different kind of paragraph.
Write a short answer to each question first. If a short answer to the second question is 'No, not all', you have your thesis.
Check that the two answers fit together logically, because the essay should read as one argument and not two unrelated mini-essays.
Plan one body paragraph per question, with a main idea, an explanation and an example. Give them roughly equal length.
Check what is not asked: a two-part question does not ask for advantages and disadvantages or for a general discussion of the topic.

structure.purpose: Show that you will answer both questions, and give a short answer to each.
sentences: Background: paraphrase the topic neutrally.
Thesis: answer both questions briefly.
Outline: say that you will deal with the first question and then the second.

structure.purpose: Answer the first question fully with one main reason, explained and exemplified.
sentences: Topic sentence: the first and most important reason.
Explanation: how it works.
Example: a believable person or situation.
Result or effect: why it matters.

structure.purpose: Answer the second question with a clear judgement, supported and qualified.
sentences: Topic sentence: your answer to the second question with a concession.
Explanation: the key reasons.
Example: an illustration.
Link: the fairer or more practical alternative.

structure.purpose: Confirm both answers and show how they connect.
sentences: Summary: the answer to each question in new words.
Final judgement: a recommendation or implication.

timing.what: Plan: separate the questions, short answer to each, one example per body paragraph
Write: introduction (4), question one (9), question two (9), conclusion (3), buffer (5)
Check: both questions answered equally, thesis matches conclusion, grammar and word count

pitfalls: Answering only one question fully, or giving the second a few lines. Both questions are marked, and a partial response is limited to Band 5 or 6 in Task Response.
Writing a general essay about the topic (the history of remote work) instead of answering the specific questions asked.
Producing two separate essays that do not connect. The essay should read as a single, coherent line of thought.
Not giving a clear answer to a 'Should...?' question. Sitting on the fence without stating a position leaves Task Response unclear.
Developing only one question with an example and leaving the other as a generalisation. Undeveloped parts limit the band.
Switching person or register in the second paragraph (you should...), which affects tone and cohesion.

phrases: One of the main attractions is
In my view, employers should not
A junior analyst who ..., for example,

band8: Task Response: both questions get equally developed, specific answers, and the second answer is qualified rather than absolute (remote work where it suits the role), which shows judgement.
Coherence and Cohesion: the thesis, the two bodies and the conclusion follow the order of the questions, and the final sentence of Body 2 links the two answers together.
Lexical Resource: precise, topic-appropriate collocations (caring responsibilities, retain experienced staff, informal relationships) avoid repeating the words of the prompt.
Grammatical Range and Accuracy: relative clauses, modal verbs for recommendation and concessive clauses (While newer staff ...) used accurately and naturally throughout.
Argument quality: the example in each paragraph is concrete and its consequence is stated, so the reasoning is shown rather than assumed.

advantages.title: Task 2: Advantages and disadvantages
advantages.summary: The examiner is testing whether you give a balanced, developed treatment of both sides and read the exact wording of the question: some versions also ask whether advantages outweigh disadvantages, which requires a judgement.
steps: Underline 'advantages and disadvantages' and check the end of the question. If it adds 'Do the advantages outweigh the disadvantages?', you must give a judgement; if not, a balanced conclusion is enough.
Define the development precisely (here: AI screening applications and answering customer questions), so your points stay on this specific use and not on technology in general.
Brainstorm two or three points on each side, then select the strongest one or two for each. Choose points that can be developed with a believable example.
Decide the balance: equal weight, or one side stronger. Your conclusion should reflect that balance rather than contradict the body.
Plan the sentence flow in each body paragraph: point, explanation, example, effect. Check the example is specific to the development.

structure.purpose: Frame the development and signal that you will weigh both sides.
sentences: Background: paraphrase the development neutrally.
Thesis: name the main advantage and the main disadvantage in precise terms.
Outline: say the order you will treat them (optional).

structure.purpose: Develop the strongest advantage so that it is convincing and specific.
sentences: Topic sentence: the main advantage.
Explanation: how it works.
Example: a realistic case.
Result or effect: the benefit to people or organisations.

structure.purpose: Develop the strongest disadvantage with equal depth, starting with a clear contrast.
sentences: Topic sentence: with 'however' or similar.
Explanation: how the risk arises.
Example: a realistic case.
Result or effect: the consequence, including a possible remedy.

structure.purpose: Weigh the two sides and give a balanced, reasoned judgement.
sentences: Summary: the two main points in new words.
Final judgement: a recommendation or verdict.

timing.what: Plan: check the exact question, choose one strong point per side with an example
Write: introduction (4), advantages (9), disadvantages (9), conclusion (3), buffer (5)
Check: both sides balanced, judgement present if asked, grammar and word count

pitfalls: Writing about only one side, or giving the second side a single sentence. The question asks for both, so imbalance caps Task Response.
Ignoring a final 'outweigh' question. If it is asked, a conclusion without a judgement is a partial answer.
Writing about technology in general rather than the specific development named in the question. Off-topic ideas lose Task Response marks.
Listing points with no explanation ('It is faster. It is cheaper. It is easier'). Short assertions are undeveloped and read as Band 5 to 6.
Using 'advantage' and 'disadvantage' as the only vocabulary. Limited range of vocabulary caps Lexical Resource.
Contradictory conclusions: weighing the disadvantages as serious in the body and then claiming advantages clearly outweigh them. Coherence and consistency are lost.
band8: Task Response: both sides are developed to a consequence, and a final judgement is balanced and conditional (use as assistants, with oversight), showing evaluation instead of repetition.
Coherence and Cohesion: the shift from advantages to disadvantages is signalled clearly and each body paragraph ends with its effect, so the essay builds a balanced argument.
Lexical Resource: precise vocabulary (screen candidates, historical data, human oversight, erode trust) with natural collocations and no repetition of 'advantage' and 'disadvantage'.
Grammatical Range and Accuracy: subordinate clauses of reason and concession, conditionals and passives used accurately, with a mix of simple and complex sentences.
Argument quality: the disadvantage includes a realistic remedy or limit, which shows critical thinking beyond listing.

task1-pie.title: Task 1: Pie chart reports
task1-pie.summary: Pie charts show shares of a whole, so the skill is comparing proportions, ranks and changes between pies rather than reading slices one at a time. Strong reports show which shares moved, which stayed stable and when the order changed.
steps: Check what the whole is (all electricity, all spending, all students) and the unit. Every pie totals 100 per cent, so describe share or proportion, not amount, unless the chart gives totals.
If there are several pies, decide whether you are comparing time (1995, 2005, 2020) or places. Time means trend language; places mean comparative language.
Rank the slices in each pie and note any change of first place, last place or order. A rank change is usually your strongest overview point.
Find which slices changed a lot and which stayed nearly constant. These two groups are the natural body paragraphs.
Write the overview as two sentences without numbers: the biggest shift, then the stable or contrasting items. Then pick only the figures that prove them.

structure.purpose: Paraphrase what the pies show, naming the whole, the categories and the years or places, with no data.
sentences: Paraphrase: change "show" to compare, "proportion" to share, and "generated" to produced.

structure.purpose: Give the main change in the shares and one contrast, with no numbers.
sentences: Overview: main feature: the item that grew or shrank most, or the change in rank.
Overview: second feature: items that stayed stable, or a stand-out contrast.

structure.purpose: Report the slices that changed most, tracing every pie in one sentence chain.
sentences: Topic sentence: name the group and its direction.
Key figures: the values in order across the pies, such as "48 per cent in 1995, 36 per cent in 2005 and 9 per cent in 2020".
Comparison: contrast with the slice moving the other way.
Trend detail: note the rank change that results.

structure.purpose: Report the remaining slices, summarising stable ones as a range instead of repeating each value.
sentences: Topic sentence: introduce the steadier group.
Key figures: exact values for the one that changed a little.
Comparison: summarise others as "within a narrow range of 14 to 16 per cent".
Closing detail: give the final ranking in the latest pie.

timing.what: Analyse the visual, choose the overview features and decide the grouping
Write: introduction and overview first (4 minutes), then two body paragraphs
Check units, figures, tenses, and that the overview contains no numbers

pitfalls: Describing each pie separately in three paragraphs. This hides the changes between pies and reads like three mini-reports, which weakens Coherence and Task Achievement.
Writing "number" or "amount" for a percentage. A pie shows share, so a slice can fall in share while the real quantity rises. Use share, proportion or percentage.
Saying a small slice "increased by 4 per cent" when it rose 4 percentage points. Use "percentage points" for the gap between two percentages.
Missing the rank change. If renewables overtake coal, that is the main point; leaving it out loses the insight examiners look for in Band 7 and above.
Ignoring that values must sum to 100. If a slice rises, others must fall, so check that your claims about the rest of the pie are consistent.
Explaining why shares changed (government policy, new technology). The task is to report what the data show, not to invent causes.

phrases: stayed within a narrow range of

band8: Task Achievement: the overview names the biggest shift and a rank change, and the body groups slices by pattern of change rather than by pie.
Task Achievement: stable slices are summarised as a range or a single phrase, which shows selection. Band 7 often gives every value.
Coherence and Cohesion: values for one slice are traced across all pies in one sentence, and contrast words (by contrast, whereas) join the opposing slices.

Lexical Resource and Grammatical Range: varied share verbs (accounted for, supplied, made up) and approximation, with participle clauses such as "having replaced coal" and accurate use of per cent and percentage points.

task1-table.title: Task 1: Table reports
task1-table.summary: A table is full of numbers and has no obvious shape, so the examiner is looking at how you choose. Find the highest, lowest and the patterns across rows and columns, then compare rather than list.
steps: Read the title, column headings, units and date. Units often differ by column (millions, per cent, pounds), and each figure needs its own unit.
Scan down every column for the highest and lowest row, and mark them. These extremes are your most reliable material.
Scan across rows to see how the columns relate. Look for a relationship such as high visitors with low spending, or a row that is highest in one column and lowest in another.
Decide the grouping: rows that behave alike, a top group and a bottom group, or two contrasting columns. A row or column that fits no group can be left out.
Write the overview with the pattern or relationship and one or two stand-out rows, without numbers, then choose only the figures that support it.

structure.purpose: Say what the table compares, naming the rows and the measures, in one paraphrased sentence.
sentences: Paraphrase: "gives information about" becomes compares; list the measures as "in terms of".

structure.purpose: State the pattern across the table and the most striking rows.
sentences: Overview: main feature: the relationship between columns, or the leader and the laggard.
Overview: second feature: one or two stand-out rows contrasted.

structure.purpose: Report the first group of rows, moving across the columns for the main row.
sentences: Topic sentence: name the group by what its rows share.
Key figures: figures for the leading row with units.
Comparison: the same row in another column, or against another row.
Trend detail: a further figure that supports the pattern.

structure.purpose: Report the contrasting group, linking back to Body 1.
sentences: Topic sentence: the contrasting group and how it differs.
Key figures: the leading row of this group.
Comparison: a second row at the other extreme.
Closing detail: a final superlative in a column not yet used.

timing.what: Analyse the visual, choose the overview features and decide the grouping
Write: introduction and overview first (4 minutes), then two body paragraphs
Check units, figures, tenses, and that the overview contains no numbers

pitfalls: Describing the table cell by cell or row by row. This is a list of numbers, not a summary, and it limits Task Achievement and Coherence at Band 6.
Treating a table like a trend graph. Without dates in columns there is nothing to "increase" or "decrease"; use comparative and superlative language instead.
Mixing up units, such as writing 6.5 million as 6.5 thousand, or putting "per cent" after a price. Accuracy of data is part of Task Achievement.
Reporting only one column. Examiners look for movement across columns, so link at least two measures for the key rows.
Using "the most" without checking the whole column. A claim of highest or lowest must be true for every row in that column.
Giving reasons for the figures. The table does not explain why a city is busy or expensive, so explanations are unsupported and penalised.

phrases: the gap between X and Y

band8: Task Achievement: the overview identifies a relationship between columns, not just the largest row, and the body selects rows that prove it.
Task Achievement: some cells and some rows are deliberately left out. A Band 7 answer often reports every row once.
Coherence and Cohesion: each body paragraph has a theme (busy and cheap, quiet and expensive) and reference words connect sentences.
Lexical Resource and Grammatical Range: varied superlatives and comparatives, accurate units, and sentences that combine three facts about one row using relative and participle clauses.

task1-map.title: Task 1: Map reports
task1-map.summary: Map tasks test whether you can describe location and change accurately. Examiners look for compass and relative position language, the passive voice, changes grouped by area, and an overview of the overall transformation.
steps: Orient yourself first: north is the top of the map. Choose two or three fixed features (river, main road, coast) to use as reference points for every location.
Compare the maps feature by feature and note each one as added, removed, replaced, extended, moved or unchanged. Note the unchanged ones too, because they belong in the overview.
Count the changes. Aim to report five to eight clearly, and group them by area (north and south, inland and coast) or by type (housing, leisure, transport).
Decide the overview: what kind of change it is overall (more developed, more urban, more tourist-oriented) and what stayed the same.

Choose your tense: past for the earlier map, present perfect or past simple for the change, present simple for the later map if it is "now". Plan passive sentences, because things are built, replaced and cleared.

structure.purpose: Say which place the maps show and the time frame, in different words from the question.
sentences: Paraphrase: "maps show" becomes illustrate; "today" becomes the present day.

structure.purpose: Summarise the overall transformation and what stayed the same, with no detailed location.
sentences: Overview: main feature: the general direction of change (more developed, built up, modernised).
Overview: second feature: the fixed geography or features that did not change.

structure.purpose: Report the changes in the first area, using compass directions and fixed reference points.
sentences: Topic sentence: name the area and the type of change.
Change detail: one change with location, before and after.
Change detail: a second change linked to the first by "in addition" or a relative clause.

structure.purpose: Report the changes in the second area, so the two paragraphs together cover every important change.
sentences: Topic sentence: the second area and its type of change.
Change detail: the main change with a position relative to a fixed feature.
Change detail: a further change with direction of extension or movement.
Change detail: a final change, ending the report.

timing.what: Analyse the visual, choose the overview features and decide the grouping
Write: introduction and overview first (4 minutes), then two body paragraphs
Check units, figures, tenses, and that the overview contains no numbers

pitfalls: Describing the first map in one paragraph and the second in another. The task is about change, so each sentence should connect then and now.
Using vague location such as "on the left" or "near the top". Use north, south, east, west, north-east and relative phrases such as "between the road and the beach".
Mixing up compass directions. North is the top; east is the right. A wrong direction is an accuracy error that cannot be corrected by good grammar.
Using the active voice for every change ("they built a bridge"). The passive ("a bridge was built") is the natural form and shows grammatical range.
Omitting the features that did not change. Examiners expect the overview to mention both the transformation and the constants.
Giving reasons or opinions (the village needed more housing; this is better for tourists). Only report what the maps show.

phrases: to the south of the main road
between the road and the beach
was cleared to make way for

band8: Task Achievement: the overview states the nature of the overall transformation and the constants. Band 7 may only describe changes in detail.
Coherence and Cohesion: changes are grouped by area or type, with each location tied to a fixed reference point such as the river or main road.
Lexical Resource: a wide range of change verbs (replaced, converted, cleared, enlarged, extended) rather than "built" and "removed" repeated.
Grammatical Range and Accuracy: accurate passives in present perfect and past simple, relative clauses for location, and correct compass directions throughout.

task1-mixed.title: Task 1: Mixed visual reports
task1-mixed.summary: When two different visuals appear together, the examiner checks that you cover both, use the right language for each and link them into one coherent report. One overview must cover both.
steps: Identify what each visual shows (a trend, a share, a comparison) and how they relate: the same topic, the same year, or the same group of people.
Analyse each separately for two or three key features: the biggest trend or difference and one contrast. Do not try to match every figure from one visual with the other.
Look for a link: a visual may give the totals, the other the breakdown, or one may show change over time while the other shows a snapshot. Decide how to signal this.
Plan one body paragraph per visual, or group by theme if the visuals overlap. Each body paragraph needs its own topic sentence naming its visual.
Write the overview as two sentences, one from each visual, joined with "at the same time" or "while", and without numbers.

structure.purpose: Paraphrase both visuals in one or two sentences, naming each visual and the topic they share.
sentences: Paraphrase: join the two visuals with "while" or "and", and change the verb for each.

structure.purpose: Give the main feature from each visual in a single overview that reads as one story.
sentences: Overview: main feature: the key trend or difference in the first visual.
Overview: second feature: the key trend or difference in the second visual.

structure.purpose: Report the first visual with selected figures and a comparison.
sentences: Topic sentence: name the visual and the group of data.
Key figures: exact values for the main item.
Comparison: contrast with another item, using trend language for a graph.

structure.purpose: Report the second visual and link it to the first.
sentences: Topic sentence: signpost the second visual and the contrast it brings.
Key figures: the two most important changes or differences, with units.
Closing detail: a final rank or constant, ending the report.

timing.what: Analyse the visual, choose the overview features and decide the grouping
Write: introduction and overview first (4 minutes), then two body paragraphs
Check units, figures, tenses, and that the overview contains no numbers

pitfalls: Describing only one visual in detail and the other in a single sentence. Both visuals carry marks, so each needs a balanced body paragraph.
Failing to link the visuals. Two unrelated paragraphs read like two separate answers; a shared overview and a signposting phrase make them one report.
Claiming one visual causes the other (more leisure travel caused more flights). Unless the data say so, report each pattern and let the reader draw links.
Using the wrong language for the visual: trend verbs for a pie chart with one year, or "proportion" language for a line graph in millions.
Overloading the report with figures from both visuals. You are expected to select, so be stricter than for a single visual.
Forgetting to mention units and time frames for each visual, since they can differ between a graph and a table.

phrases: The table provides further detail on

language.use: Share language for charts and tables

phrases: the most noticeable feature in both

band8: Task Achievement: both visuals are covered in a single overview, and the key feature of each is selected. Band 7 often has an overview for only one.
Coherence and Cohesion: each body paragraph is devoted to a visual with a signpost, and linking phrases connect the two.
Lexical Resource: language is matched to the visual (trend verbs for the graph, share verbs for the pies) and paraphrase is varied.
Grammatical Range and Accuracy: sentences combine trend and comparison in one structure, with accurate tenses and no causal claims that the data cannot support.
